claims.text: Superconductivity in the proposed uncharacterized high-entropy alloy is governed by the degree of local chemical short-range order within its disordered matrix.
Local enrichment of superconductivity-favorable elements enhances electron-phonon coupling.
The starting material is an equimolar alloy containing at least five elements, each at no less than 5 atomic percent.
The starting material is a fully disordered, single-phase solid solution.
Controlled annealing can induce moderate short-range order without precipitating secondary phases.
Annealing at approximately 0.5 times the melting temperature under an inert atmosphere can preserve the single-phase solid-solution state.
Annealing produces local clusters enriched in elements favorable for electron-phonon interactions.
Localized short-range order alters the electronic density of states.
Concentrating elements with stronger electron-phonon coupling enhances the superconducting pairing potential.
Short-range order induced by annealing increases the superconducting transition temperature relative to the fully random alloy.
The annealed alloy will exhibit measurable electronic-density-of-states shifts consistent with enhanced electron-phonon coupling.
The as-cast baseline has a uniform random distribution of all constituent elements.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a single-phase solid solution and excludes samples that undergo phase segregation or precipitation.
Residual strain or incipient segregation may also influence superconductivity.
